statement: More frequent Finnish sauna bathing is associated with substantially lower cardiovascular and all-cause mortality in a dose-dependent fashion: 4-7 sessions/week vs 1/week had ~40% lower all-cause and ~50% lower fatal-CVD mortality.
effect_size: 4-7x/week vs 1x/week: all-cause mortality HR ~0.60; fatal CVD HR ~0.50; sudden cardiac death HR ~0.37. Longer single sessions also lower risk.
population: 2,315 middle-aged Finnish men, KIHD prospective cohort, ~20y follow-up

provenance.primary: Laukkanen, Laukkanen et al. — 'Association Between Sauna Bathing and Fatal Cardiovascular and All-Cause Mortality Events', JAMA Internal Medicine 2015

confidence_notes: Observational. Healthy-user bias and reverse causation (sick men sauna less) are NOT excluded; no RCT exists. Direction is strong and dose-dependent but causality is unproven. Men-only cohort.

statement: Frequent sauna bathing is associated with lower incidence of dementia and Alzheimer's disease in the same Finnish cohort.
population: 2,315 middle-aged Finnish men, KIHD cohort, ~20y follow-up

provenance.primary: Laukkanen et al. — 'Sauna bathing is inversely associated with dementia and Alzheimer's disease in middle-aged Finnish men', Age and Ageing 2016

confidence_notes: Same cohort/limitations as the mortality finding. Association only; mechanism (cardiovascular, HSP, relaxation) is hypothesized not proven.

statement: Sauna heat exposure acutely raises heart rate, cardiac output and skin blood flow and lowers blood pressure, producing a cardiovascular load and post-session vasodilation broadly comparable to moderate exercise; repeated exposure is proposed to improve endothelial function.
effect_size: HR rises to ~100-150 bpm; transient BP changes; improved arterial compliance proposed.

provenance.primary: Laukkanen & Kunutsor — 'Cardiovascular and Other Health Benefits of Sauna Bathing: A Review of the Evidence', Mayo Clinic Proceedings 2018

confidence_notes: Mechanism/physiology. The 'sauna mimics exercise' framing is partially supported but should not be read as equivalence for fitness outcomes.

statement: Heat stress induces heat-shock proteins (HSPs, e.g. HSP70/HSP90) that act as molecular chaperones supporting proteostasis, and underlies physiological heat acclimation (plasma-volume expansion, earlier sweating, lower thermal strain).
effect_size: Upregulated HSP expression + integrated thermoregulatory/cardiovascular acclimation adaptations.

provenance.primary: Periard, Racinais, Sawka — 'Adaptations and mechanisms of human heat acclimation', Scand J Med Sci Sports 2015

confidence_notes: MECHANISM — HSP induction is real; the leap from 'sauna raises HSPs' to 'sauna extends lifespan' is exactly the mechanism->outcome gap the schema forbids conflating. Cross-links to the proteostasis aging hallmark (Domain B).

statement: Functional, cold-activated brown adipose tissue (BAT) exists in adult humans (not just infants) and is recruited by cold exposure, demonstrated independently by three 2009 studies using FDG-PET/CT.
effect_size: Cold-stimulated BAT detectable in the large majority of healthy adults; activity inversely related to BMI/age.
population: Healthy adults (3 independent human imaging studies)

provenance.primary: van Marken Lichtenbelt et al. (NEJM 2009, 10.1056/NEJMoa0808718); Cypess et al. (NEJM 2009, 10.1056/NEJMoa0810780); Virtanen et al. (NEJM 2009, 10.1056/NEJMoa0808949)
provenance.surfaced_via: OpenAlex direct-DOI cold BAT NEJM x3

confidence_notes: Mechanism, replicated. Establishes the SUBSTRATE for cold-thermogenesis claims. Does NOT by itself establish metabolic-disease or longevity outcomes.

statement: Acute cold-water immersion sharply raises plasma norepinephrine (and metabolic rate via shivering and non-shivering/BAT thermogenesis); cold immersion increased norepinephrine roughly 2-5x in human studies.
effect_size: Cold (14 C) immersion: norepinephrine ~+530%, dopamine ~+250%; metabolic rate rises (shivering > non-shivering at acute exposure).

provenance.primary: Sramek et al. — 'Human physiological responses to immersion into water of different temperatures', Eur J Appl Physiol 2000

confidence_notes: MECHANISM ONLY. 'Cold raises norepinephrine' is the most-laundered claim in cold-exposure media — it is NOT 'cold improves mood/focus/longevity' as an outcome. Acute thermogenesis is dominated by shivering; non-shivering/BAT contribution grows with acclimation.

statement: Repeated cold exposure (cold acclimation) shifts thermogenesis from shivering toward non-shivering (BAT-mediated) thermogenesis and recruits BAT — a genuine adaptive remodeling of how the body produces heat.
effect_size: Acclimation increases BAT volume/activity and non-shivering capacity; reduces reliance on shivering at a given cold load.
population: Winter swimmers vs controls; cold-acclimation human studies

provenance.primary: Soberg et al. — 'Altered brown fat thermoregulation and enhanced cold-induced thermogenesis in young, healthy, winter-swimming men', Cell Reports Medicine 2021

confidence_notes: Mechanism. Winter-swimmer study is small and combines cold + heat (sauna) exposure, complicating attribution. Adaptive thermogenesis is real; metabolic-health OUTCOMES are a separate, weaker claim.

statement: Ten days of mild cold acclimation improved peripheral insulin sensitivity in patients with type 2 diabetes, associated with increased skeletal-muscle GLUT4 translocation (largely independent of classical BAT).
effect_size: ~43% increase in insulin-stimulated glucose uptake after 10 days of cold acclimation.
population: Small intervention study, patients with type 2 diabetes

provenance.primary: Hanssen et al. — 'Short-term cold acclimation improves insulin sensitivity in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus', Nature Medicine 2015

confidence_notes: A real human OUTCOME (surrogate: insulin sensitivity, not hard endpoints). Small n, short duration, uses prolonged mild cold (hours/day at ~14-15 C) — NOT the 'cold plunge' protocol popularly marketed.

statement: A randomized trial of routine cold (or cold-finishing) showering reduced self-reported sickness absence from work, though it did not reduce the number of sick days per illness episode.
effect_size: ~29% reduction in sickness-absence; no change in illness-day count per episode; quality-of-life/energy self-reports improved.
population: 3,018 adults, randomized to 30-90s cold shower vs control, Netherlands

provenance.primary: Buijze et al. — 'The Effect of Cold Showering on Health and Work: A Randomized Controlled Trial', PLoS ONE 2016

confidence_notes: Rare ACTUAL RCT in this space. Self-reported outcomes, unblinded, no biological mechanism confirmed; the absence reduction without fewer sick-days-per-illness is hard to interpret (possible behavioral/expectancy effect).

statement: Thermal stress (heat and cold), like exercise and fasting, is framed as a hormetic stressor: a sub-damaging dose triggers adaptive stress-response programs (HSPs, antioxidant defenses, mitochondrial/thermogenic remodeling) that confer net benefit, while excessive dose is harmful.
effect_size: Dose-response is biphasic (J/U-shaped) by hypothesis; the beneficial dose window is not precisely defined for humans.

provenance.primary: Hormesis framework (Calabrese; mitohormesis: Ristow) applied to thermal stress; synthesized across Laukkanen (heat), Soberg/Hanssen (cold)
provenance.surfaced_via: cross-cutting thread from IDEAL-STATE-MAP (hormesis unifies thermal/exercise/fasting)

confidence_notes: FRAMEWORK/HYPOTHESIS, not an outcome. Useful organizing lens but risks being unfalsifiable if used to explain any result post hoc. The human beneficial-dose window for cold/heat is genuinely unknown.
